title: Detect Cycle
description: Floyd tortoise-and-hare: two pointers move at 1x and 2x speed. If they ever meet, there is a cycle. O(n) time, O(1) space.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: I'm given the head of a singly linked list and I need to return true if any node's `next` pointer creates a cycle back to an earlier node, false otherwise. So the list is either acyclic and ends in null, or it loops back somewhere — possibly at the head (full loop) or deeper in the list (lollipop shape)."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Empty list — return false (no nodes, no cycle)?
• Single node with `next = null` → false; single node pointing at itself → true. Both possible?
• Can I mutate the input (mark nodes as visited)? Or do I need to leave it untouched?
• Memory budget — is O(n) extra space fine, or do you want O(1)?
sections.why: The mutation and memory questions point at the answer. If you can mutate, you could mark visited nodes with a flag — O(n) time, O(1) extra space but destructive. If you can use O(n) extra space, a Set of visited nodes is the obvious answer. If neither is allowed — leave nodes untouched, O(1) space — you're forced into Floyd's tortoise-and-hare, which is the canonical answer interviewers are usually fishing for. Asking surfaces all three solutions cleanly.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(n) extra-space solution before you discard it.
sections.say: "The obvious solution is a hash Set: walk the list, and at each node check if I've seen it before. If I have, return true. If I hit null, return false. That's O(n) time but O(n) extra space because the Set can hold up to n nodes. Functionally correct, but I think we can do it in O(1) space — same correctness, but with two pointers instead of a Set."
sections.why: Two reasons to name the Set version out loud. (1) It proves you can solve the problem without the trick — interviewers worry about candidates who only know Floyd's and can't reason from first principles. (2) It frames Floyd's as 'same correctness guarantee, less memory' rather than a wholly different idea — which justifies the cleverness instead of just deploying it. The interviewer might even say 'Set is fine, ship it,' in which case you've saved time.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to Floyd's tortoise-and-hare?
sections.say:
"This is the canonical fast-and-slow pointer problem. The insight is: if there's a cycle, a pointer moving at 2x speed eventually laps a pointer moving at 1x speed inside that cycle — they MUST meet, because the gap between them closes by 1 node per iteration once they're both inside the loop. If there's no cycle, the fast pointer hits null first (specifically, `fast` or `fast.next` becomes null) and we exit. Two pointers moving at the SAME speed wouldn't work — they'd maintain a fixed gap forever. The 2-to-1 step ratio is what guarantees they collide inside any cycle.

Two things to be careful about: the loop guard checks BOTH `fast` AND `fast.next` because fast does a double-hop and both `.next` accesses have to be legal. And the meeting check uses `===` (reference equality on the node object), not `slow.val === fast.val` — different nodes can hold the same value."
sections.why: Naming the pattern *and* the mathematical reason it works is the move. 'Floyd's tortoise-and-hare' alone is just terminology; 'they collide because the 2-to-1 step ratio means the gap closes by 1 each iteration once both are in the loop' is a derivation. Calling out the `===` vs `.val` distinction upfront also short-circuits the most common bug — values can repeat across distinct nodes, so value equality would give false positives.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure the model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — a small cycle at the head, an acyclic list where fast hits null, and a 2-node self-loop to confirm the smallest possible cycle works.

examples.note: Classic cycle — fast laps slow on the second pass.
examples.trace:
init: slow=node#0(1), fast=node#0(1)
iter1: slow=node#1(2), fast=node#2(3). slow !== fast.
iter2: slow=node#2(3), fast=node#1(2). slow !== fast. (fast wrapped: 3→1→2)
iter3: slow=node#0(1), fast=node#0(1). slow === fast → return true.

examples.note: Acyclic — fast hits the end first. Loop guard catches `fast.next === null` and exits.
examples.trace:
init: slow=node#0(1), fast=node#0(1)
iter1: slow=node#1(2), fast=node#2(3). slow !== fast.
iter2: slow=node#2(3), fast=node#4(5). slow !== fast.
loop guard: fast=node#4(5), fast.next=null → false. Exit loop.
return false.

examples.note: Smallest cycle — fast laps slow in one iteration.
examples.trace:
init: slow=node#0(1), fast=node#0(1)
iter1: slow=node#1(2), fast=node#1(2). (fast: 1→2→1→2, lands on 2.) slow === fast → return true.

sections.why: Tracing surfaces two bugs this problem rewards. (1) The acyclic case confirms the loop guard `fast && fast.next` is the right condition — if you only checked `fast`, the `fast.next.next` would throw on a single-step-from-null. (2) The 1→2→1 trace confirms that fast can land on the same node as slow in a single iteration when the cycle is small enough; without tracing, candidates sometimes think the meeting only happens after multiple wraps and get confused when it fires immediately. Worth verifying on the whiteboard before the interviewer points to a test case where slow and fast collide in iter 1.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Empty list (head = null) → loop guard `fast && fast.next` is false immediately, return false. ✓
• Single node, no cycle (head.next = null) → loop guard `fast.next` is false, return false. ✓
• Single node, self-loop (head.next = head) → first iteration: slow = head.next = head, fast = head.next.next = head. slow === fast, return true. ✓
• Cycle at head (full loop, like 1→2→3→1) → handled — fast laps slow inside the cycle eventually.
• Cycle deep in the list (lollipop, like 1→2→3→4→3) → also handled — slow walks the straight part first, then both end up in the cycle and fast catches up.
• Very large list → O(n) time, O(1) space; no risk of memory blow-up.
• Worth noting: this returns *whether* a cycle exists, not *where* it starts. The 'find the cycle's entry node' variant (LeetCode 142) is a follow-up that reuses the same meeting point with a clever second-pass trick."
sections.why: The self-loop edge is the one most candidates miss — they assume cycles have at least two distinct nodes. Walking through it on the whiteboard confirms the algorithm handles it without a special case. The lollipop case is also worth naming because it disproves a common misconception that 'fast and slow have to start at the cycle entry to collide' — they don't; fast catches up regardless. Flagging the LeetCode 142 follow-up unprompted shows you see the cycle-detection family, not just this one problem.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n) — the gap between slow and fast closes by 1 node per iteration once both are in the cycle, so they meet within at most C iterations where C is the cycle length. Before the cycle, slow walks at most n nodes to reach it. Total: bounded by 2n iterations, so O(n). For the acyclic case, fast hits null in at most n/2 iterations, also O(n).

Space is O(1) — two pointer variables, no auxiliary structure. This is what beats the hash-Set version.

If you wanted to extend to 'find the cycle's starting node' (LeetCode 142), it's the same two-pointer setup with a clever second phase: after slow and fast meet, reset one pointer to head and advance both at 1x — they meet again at the cycle entry. The math is from Floyd's full algorithm: distance from head to cycle entry equals distance from meeting point to cycle entry going forward. Same template, one extra walk."
sections.why: The amortized 2n bound is the right defense against an interviewer who pushes back with 'but slow and fast are both walking — isn't that more than n?'. The answer is that the gap closes by 1 per iteration, so even with the 2x speed difference, fast traverses at most 2n nodes total. The LeetCode 142 extension is the natural next problem and proves you see the slow/fast template as a family rather than a one-off — that's how it shows up in Find Duplicate Number, Linked List Cycle II, and Happy Number.

walkthrough.intro: Step through Floyd tortoise-and-hare. Input is { values, cycleAt }: cycleAt = index where the last node loops back, or -1 for no cycle. Watch slow advance by 1 and fast by 2 — if they meet, return true.
trace: const nodes = values.map((v) => ({ val: v, next: null }));
for (let i = 0; i < nodes.length - 1; i++) nodes[i].next = nodes[i + 1];
yield { line: 1, label: `enter function — values=${JSON.stringify(values)}, cycleAt=${cycleAt}`, state: { values, cycleAt } };
yield { line: 2, label: `init slow=${id(slow)}, fast=${id(fast)}`, state: { slow: id(slow), fast: id(fast) } };
yield { line: 3, label: `loop guard ok (iter ${iter}) — fast and fast.next both non-null`, state: { iter, slow: id(slow), fast: id(fast) } };
yield { line: 4, label: `slow +1 → ${id(slow)}`, state: { iter, slow: id(slow), fast: id(fast) } };
yield { line: 5, label: `fast +2 → ${id(fast)}`, state: { iter, slow: id(slow), fast: id(fast) } };
yield { line: 6, label: `slow === fast — cycle detected, return true`, state: { iter, slow: id(slow), fast: id(fast), returns: true } };
yield { line: 6, label: `slow !== fast — keep going`, state: { iter, slow: id(slow), fast: id(fast) } };
if (iter > 50) { yield { line: 3, label: 'safety stop', state: { returns: false } }; return; }
yield { line: 8, label: `loop exit — fast or fast.next is null, return false`, state: { iter, slow: id(slow), fast: id(fast), returns: false } };

notes: Loop condition checks BOTH fast and fast.next — fast moves 2, so both hops must be legal.
Compare with === (reference equality on the node object), not by .val.
Hash-set approach also works in O(n) time but uses O(n) space. Floyd is the canonical O(1)-space.

questions.q: Why must the loop check both `fast` AND `fast.next`?
options: Checking just `fast.next` is enough — if `fast` were null, `fast.next` would already throw
fast moves two steps; both .next hops must be non-null
To match the loop condition slow uses, keeping the two pointer walks symmetric
Without the `fast` check, slow could overtake fast and cause an infinite loop

questions.q: Space complexity of Floyd cycle detection?
options: O(log n)
O(n)

questions.q: How do slow and fast compare when checking for a meeting?
options: By .val (value equality)
By === (reference equality on the node)
By position index
By .next pointer

questions.q: If there is no cycle, the loop ends because:
options: slow reaches the tail node first and triggers a `slow.next === null` exit
fast or fast.next becomes null
fast eventually points back at the head, which the loop treats as a sentinel
slow and fast converge on the tail and pass the `slow === fast` check

questions.q: Once both pointers are inside the cycle, why are they guaranteed to meet?
options: They start at the same node
The gap between them shrinks by exactly 1 node each iteration, so it eventually hits 0
fast resets to slow's position periodically
The cycle length is always even
questions.explain: Fast gains 1 net node on slow per step (2 minus 1), so the gap modulo the cycle length decreases by 1 each iteration until it reaches 0 — a collision.

questions.q: If both pointers moved at the SAME speed (slow +1, fast +1), would cycle detection still work?
options: Yes, they would still meet
No — they keep a fixed gap forever and never collide inside the cycle
Yes, but only for even-length cycles
No — they would both immediately point to null
questions.explain: Equal speed means the gap never changes, so they never close in; the 2-to-1 ratio is what forces the gap to shrink to 0.

questions.q: What is Floyd's main advantage over storing visited nodes in a Set?
options: It is asymptotically faster in time
It uses O(1) space instead of O(n)
It handles unsorted lists
It can find the cycle length
questions.explain: Both are O(n) time, but the Set holds up to n nodes (O(n) space) while Floyd uses only two pointers (O(1) space).

questions.q: Why compare nodes with `slow === fast` rather than `slow.val === fast.val`?
options: === is faster than .val comparison
Distinct nodes can hold equal values, so value equality would give false positives
.val might be undefined
Reference equality skips the head node
questions.explain: Two different nodes can share the same value; only reference equality confirms the pointers landed on the same node.

questions.q: To find WHERE the cycle starts (LeetCode 142), after slow and fast meet you:
options: Return the meeting node directly
Reset one pointer to head, then advance both by 1 — they meet at the cycle entry
Count nodes until fast wraps again
Reverse the list from the meeting point
questions.explain: Floyd's math: the head-to-entry distance equals the meeting-point-to-entry distance, so two 1-step walkers from head and meeting point converge at the entry.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the tortoise-and-hare loop. Build a 3-node cycle a → b → c → a.

blanks.hint: guard the second hop — both must be legal
fast moves by two — the FULL double-hop expression
reference equality on the node object, not .val

L3.prompt: Write `hasCycle(head)` using Floyd two-pointer (O(1) space). Build a 2-node cycle a → b → a and log `hasCycle(a)`.
hints: Two pointers from head — slow +1, fast +2.
Loop while fast AND fast.next are truthy.
If they ever meet (===), return true.
